units: Data types, constants, input and output, MOD/DIV, arithmetic, strings and casting
The lessons use OCR Exam Reference Language (ERL), a form of pseudocode. Real programming languages may use different syntax. Learn the logic, and recognise equivalent Python statements.
Integer: whole numbers. Real/float: numbers with a fractional part. Boolean: True or False. Character: one character. String: a sequence of zero or more characters.
A variable is a named value that can change while the program runs. Assignment uses = in the OCR examples, e.g. lives = lives - 1. The value on the right is evaluated before it is stored on the left.
A constant is a named value that should not change while a program runs, e.g. const MAX_CAPACITY = 12. Constants make code easier to read and prevent accidental changes.
An input statement receives data, processing uses calculations or decisions, and output presents results. In Python input() returns text, so int() or float() may be needed before arithmetic.
Addition +, subtraction -, multiplication *, division / and exponentiation ^ are used in ERL. Brackets and standard precedence decide the order of calculation.
DIV produces an integer quotient and MOD produces the remainder. Example: 29 DIV 6 = 4 and 29 MOD 6 = 5. Python uses // and % for equivalent positive-integer cases.
int(), float(), str() and other conversion functions change representations. ASC('D') yields 68 and CHR(68) yields 'D'. Use conversions when combining text and numeric values.
Concatenation joins strings, e.g. 'cat' + 'fish' gives 'catfish'. Strings also support length, substring, left, right and changing case; exact syntax and substring parameters depend on the language.
Comments explain intent, structure and non-obvious decisions. OCR pseudocode uses //, while Python uses #. They are not instructions to execute.
Sequence, IF/ELSE, nested decisions, comparisons, Boolean operators and random numbers
Sequence runs instructions in order. Selection chooses a branch using a condition. Iteration repeats code. All three are used to construct algorithms.
Instructions run from top to bottom until a branch or loop changes the flow. Example: subtotal = 20; discount = 3; final = subtotal - discount; print(final).
IF tests a condition and chooses which statements execute. ELSE provides an alternative, while ELSEIF tests further conditions in order.
Use == for equality in Python-like comparisons, != for not equal, > and < for greater/less, >= and <= for inclusive comparisons. Assignment and comparison are different operations.
AND is True only if both conditions are True; OR is True if at least one is True; NOT reverses a Boolean value. Brackets can make complex conditions clearer.
An IF statement can contain another IF. For example, a discounted ticket price may depend on both age group and whether a day is a weekend.
A switch/case structure selects between several possible cases. It may be clearer than many ELSEIF branches when checking one value against several alternatives.
The reference examples introduce random number generation. In Python random.randint(1,6) gives whole numbers from 1 to 6 inclusive, representing a fair six-sided die.
Check values exactly at a threshold, not only clearly above or below it. A comparison such as mark >= 60 includes 60, whereas mark > 60 does not.
FOR, WHILE and DO UNTIL, conditions tested at different stages and infinite loops
Iteration repeats a group of instructions without copying the same code many times. The condition or counter determines when repetition stops.
A FOR loop is useful for a known number of repetitions. In the taught pseudocode, FOR n = 1 TO 5 performs five passes (1,2,3,4,5). The Python equivalent is range(1,6).
A WHILE loop checks the condition before each iteration, then executes the body only while it is True. It can run zero times if the condition is initially False.
A DO UNTIL loop executes the body and then tests its stop condition. It therefore executes at least once and repeats until its condition becomes True.
WHILE tests a continuation condition at the start. DO UNTIL tests a stopping condition at the end. Changing one into the other requires considering where the first input or action occurs.
A counter tracks the number of iterations; an accumulator stores a running total. Initialise these before the loop when their value is needed across iterations.
A loop that cannot reach its exit condition continues indefinitely. Ensure the loop variable or input changes so that its condition can eventually become False or its UNTIL condition True.
A trace table records the counter, condition result, important variables and outputs after each step. Work through the initial check and final check to avoid off-by-one mistakes.
One- and two-dimensional arrays, zero-based indices, searching and sorting
An array stores a collection of values under a single identifier. In the specification examples all values in an array have the same data type and the declared array has a fixed length.
An array element is accessed with its index, often starting at 0. A five-item array has valid indices 0,1,2,3,4. Trying index 5 would be out of range.
The slides describe fixed-size arrays and note that Python lists can grow. Python list indexing is usually zero-based, and len(items) returns the number of elements.
A loop can visit every item. For a five-item collection, a Python loop 'for i in range(len(items))' visits positions 0 to 4.
A linear search compares the target with each element in turn. It can stop as soon as a match is found; otherwise it reaches the end of the array.
Bubble sort compares neighbouring items and swaps them when they are in the wrong order. Each pass moves a larger item towards the end; repeated passes produce a sorted collection.
To swap two array entries using a temporary variable: temp = a[i]; a[i] = a[i+1]; a[i+1] = temp. Languages such as Python also support simultaneous assignment.
A 2D array has rows and columns. item[row][column] identifies one cell, for example scores[1][2] means second row, third column when indexing starts at 0.
An outer loop can visit the rows while an inner loop visits columns. To total a row, reset the running total before processing the next row.
Subroutines, arguments and parameters, return values, local and global scope
A subroutine packages a named sequence of instructions. Breaking a larger program into smaller parts avoids copying code and makes it easier to test, maintain and reuse.
A procedure performs an action but does not provide a useful returned result in the taught distinction. For example, a displayMenu procedure can output several menu items.
A function performs processing and returns a value. A call such as result = square(4) can store the value returned by the function.
A parameter is a named input in the subroutine definition; an argument is the value supplied in a call. For example, function double(n) declares parameter n and double(7) passes argument 7.
A RETURN statement sends the function's result back to its caller. In a typical function, RETURN ends that call at that point.
A variable declared inside a subroutine is normally local to that call. Other functions cannot automatically read or change that local variable.
Global variables are declared outside subroutines and may be accessible more widely. Local variables are generally preferable because they reduce unintended interactions.
Variables in separate calls may have the same name but be independent. A local variable named 'score' does not have to modify a global variable with the same name.
Named subroutines reduce repetition, support separate testing, encourage reuse and make programs easier to change. Parameters let a subroutine solve a general problem for many input values.
Record fields, CSV, opening, reading, writing, appending and closing files
A record groups related fields, which can have different data types. For a book record, fields could include bookID (string), title (string), pages (integer) and available (Boolean).
A table has fields (columns) and records (rows). Each row holds information about one item; each column describes a property of those items.
A comma-separated values file is a text representation of tabular data. Each record normally appears on a new line and fields are separated by commas. Quoted fields may contain commas.
The typical steps are OPEN, READ or WRITE, and CLOSE. Closing the file finishes the operation and frees resources. In Python, a with statement can close it automatically.
Read mode loads or processes existing contents without intentionally changing them. A program may read a whole file or process one line at a time.
Write mode creates or overwrites the file's contents in common programming environments. Check the mode carefully because existing data can be replaced.
Append mode adds new data after the existing content rather than replacing previous records. It is useful when maintaining a growing log or list.
A newline character (often written \n) separates lines. When adding a new record to a text file, the program must ensure it is correctly separated from the previous record.
Python open('data.txt','x') creates a new file only if one does not already exist. This is different from write mode, which may replace an existing file.
An opened text file can be read into working memory, but the file itself remains on non-volatile secondary storage. Unsaved changes in volatile memory can be lost if power fails.
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, AND/OR, LIKE patterns, wildcard columns and ORDER BY
SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is used to work with relational databases, including retrieving records matching specified conditions.
A database table holds rows (records) and columns (fields). A field name identifies the kind of information stored in each column.
SELECT chooses which fields to display, while FROM identifies the table. Example: SELECT Title, Genre FROM Books. This displays only those two fields.
An asterisk after SELECT means all columns, not just one field. SELECT * FROM Books returns every field in each matching record.
WHERE filters rows. Example: SELECT Title FROM Books WHERE Pages > 250. Comparison operators include =, != or <>, >, <, >= and <=.
Combine criteria with AND if both conditions must hold; OR if either is sufficient. Brackets clarify the intended grouping when criteria are complex.

LIKE matches a text pattern. The supplied lesson examples use LIKE 'H*' (an Access-style wildcard). Standard SQL commonly uses LIKE 'H%' to match text starting with H. The playground accepts both so pupils can compare conventions.
ORDER BY sorts query results by a chosen field. ASC means ascending and DESC means descending. If no direction is supplied, ascending is normally used.
BETWEEN checks an inclusive range. Example: WHERE Pages BETWEEN 120 AND 300 selects rows whose Pages value is between 120 and 300, including the endpoints.

SQL injection can happen when untrusted text is inserted unsafely into a query. Applications should use parameterised queries and appropriate access controls. The revision playground runs read-only simulated queries, not unsafe database commands.
The key structure is SELECT columns FROM table WHERE criteria ORDER BY column ASC/DESC. WHERE and ORDER BY are optional. Results show selected fields from rows satisfying the criteria.

quiz.q: Which data type best stores a temperature of 18.75?
quiz.why: A real stores a fractional number.

quiz.q: What is the value of 41 DIV 6?
quiz.why: DIV returns the integer quotient.

quiz.q: What is the value of 41 MOD 6?
quiz.why: 41 = 6 × 6 + 5, so the remainder is 5.

quiz.q: What is stored in count after count = 3; count = count + 4?
quiz.why: Evaluate count + 4 and assign 7 back to count.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a constant?
options: Store a value intended to remain unchanged during execution
Store data on an optical disc
quiz.why: Constants protect named values from accidental runtime changes.

quiz.q: What is output by print('9' + '2')?
quiz.why: Concatenating two strings joins the character sequences.

quiz.q: Which function turns the text '47' into an integer?
quiz.why: int() converts suitable numeric text into an integer.

quiz.q: In the taught pseudocode, ASC('E') returns which value?
quiz.why: Uppercase E has ASCII code 69.

quiz.q: What does CHR(66) return?
quiz.why: ASCII 66 is the uppercase character B.

quiz.q: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?
quiz.why: # introduces a Python comment.

quiz.q: What is the output of print(2 + 3 * 4)?
quiz.why: Multiplication is evaluated before addition.

quiz.q: Which value is Boolean?
quiz.why: False is a Boolean; the quoted text 'False' is a string.

quiz.q: What is sequence?
options: Repeating instructions until a condition fails
Executing instructions in the order written
Storing all values in an array
quiz.why: Sequence runs the steps in order.

quiz.q: A ticket costs £3 if age < 12 and £7 otherwise. What does age 12 pay?
quiz.why: 12 is not less than 12, so the ELSE branch runs.

quiz.q: What does TRUE AND FALSE evaluate to?
quiz.why: AND needs both conditions to be True.

quiz.q: What does FALSE OR TRUE evaluate to?
quiz.why: OR is True if either condition is True.

quiz.q: What does NOT (8 >= 8) evaluate to?
quiz.why: >= is True at equality, so NOT reverses it.

quiz.q: Which comparison checks whether x is not 10?
quiz.why: != is the not-equal operator.

quiz.q: What output does IF points >= 20 THEN print('Gold') ELSE print('Silver') give for points = 20?
quiz.why: The equality case is included by >=.

quiz.q: What structure is suited to choosing from many fixed menu options?
quiz.why: A switch/case selects among named alternatives.

quiz.q: What does random.randint(1,6) return in Python?
quiz.why: Both endpoints are included.

quiz.q: Which condition requires both age >= 16 and membership to be True?
quiz.why: AND requires both conditions.

quiz.q: In a nested IF, what determines whether the inner IF executes?
options: Whether the outer branch containing it is entered
quiz.why: Nested branches are reached only through their containing branch.

quiz.q: How many times does FOR i = 2 TO 6 execute in the taught pseudocode?
quiz.why: The values are 2,3,4,5,6.

quiz.q: How many times can a WHILE loop execute if its condition starts False?
quiz.why: WHILE checks before its body.

quiz.q: How many times does a DO UNTIL body execute at minimum?
quiz.why: DO UNTIL checks its stopping condition after the body.

quiz.q: After total = 0; FOR n = 1 TO 3; total = total + n; NEXT, what is total?
quiz.why: The loop adds 1+2+3 = 6.

quiz.q: What is a counter variable?
options: A variable tracking how many iterations occurred
quiz.why: Counters often increase once per iteration.

quiz.q: What is an accumulator used for?
options: Maintaining a running result across iterations
quiz.why: An accumulator adds or combines values across passes.

quiz.q: Which loop is usually clearest for exactly 25 repetitions?
quiz.why: FOR expresses known repetition counts.

quiz.q: A WHILE loop never changes the variable tested in its condition. What could happen?
quiz.why: If the condition remains True, repetition may continue indefinitely.

quiz.q: Which condition would keep repeating while attempts is less than 4?
quiz.why: The loop continues until attempts reaches 4.

quiz.q: A loop prints 0,1,2 using FOR i = 0 TO 2. How many outputs appear?
quiz.why: The inclusive range has three values.

quiz.q: Which trace-table column helps spot an off-by-one error?
quiz.why: Recording the counter and checks reveals extra or missing iterations.

quiz.q: What is the first index in the zero-based arrays used in the lessons?
quiz.why: The first item has index 0.

quiz.q: If names has 6 items, which is its final valid index?
quiz.why: A six-item array has indices 0 through 5.

quiz.q: What is colours[2] for colours = ['red','blue','green','yellow']?
quiz.why: Index 2 is the third element.

quiz.q: Why are arrays useful?
options: They remove the need for data types
Many related values can be accessed by one identifier and an index
quiz.why: Arrays group and index related data.

quiz.q: How does a linear search find a target?
options: Split only the final two elements
Check each item in order until found or exhausted
quiz.why: Linear search examines elements sequentially.

quiz.q: Which index is accessed by marks[1][2] in a zero-based 2D array?
quiz.why: Indices start at 0 in each dimension.

quiz.q: What happens during a bubble-sort swap?
options: Two adjacent out-of-order values exchange places
The first item always becomes smallest instantly
quiz.why: Bubble sort swaps neighbouring elements that are in the wrong order.

quiz.q: Which structure suits a grid with 4 rows and 3 columns?
quiz.why: A 2D array has a row-and-column structure.

quiz.q: How many values are in a 3 by 4 2D array?
quiz.why: 3 × 4 = 12 cells.

quiz.q: Which loop pattern totals each row of a 2D array?
options: Outer loop for rows, inner loop for columns
quiz.why: Nested loops traverse rows and columns.

quiz.q: In Python, what does len(items) give?
quiz.why: len returns the collection's length.

quiz.q: What is a subroutine?
options: A named, reusable block of instructions
quiz.why: Subroutines group code under a name.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a function from a procedure in the taught model?
quiz.why: A function returns a result to its caller.

quiz.q: In function triple(n), what is n?
options: An argument supplied by a specific call
quiz.why: n is a named input in the function definition.

quiz.q: In triple(8), what is 8?
quiz.why: 8 is the value supplied to the function.

quiz.q: What should function multiply(a,b) RETURN after calculating a*b?
quiz.why: RETURN sends the result back to the caller.

quiz.q: What is the scope of a local variable inside a function?
quiz.why: Local variables belong to the subroutine's scope.

quiz.q: Why is heavy use of global variables often discouraged?
options: It is required for every function
It can create hidden interactions between program parts
quiz.why: Globals may be modified unexpectedly by unrelated code.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of separate subroutines?
options: Individual parts can be tested and reused
quiz.why: Decomposition supports testing, maintenance and reuse.

quiz.q: If function addTax(price) returns price*1.2, what does addTax(50) return?
A function has two parameters. How many arguments should a normal call supply?
quiz.why: A call normally supplies an argument for each required parameter.

quiz.q: What happens to a local variable from a finished call in the taught model?
options: It is written to a CSV
quiz.why: Locals normally belong to an active subroutine invocation.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a record?
options: One product with ID, name and price fields
quiz.why: A record groups fields that may have different data types.

quiz.q: In a table, what is a field?
quiz.why: A field describes one item of data in a record.

quiz.q: What do the letters CSV stand for?
quiz.why: CSV is a text-based format for records and fields.

quiz.q: Which operation should normally follow reading or writing a file?
quiz.why: Closing completes and frees file resources.

quiz.q: What does append mode usually do?
quiz.why: Append writes new information after the current contents.

quiz.q: What does write mode often do to an existing file?
quiz.why: Write mode often truncates existing file content.

quiz.q: Which Python mode creates a new file only if it does not already exist?
quiz.why: Exclusive creation mode x fails if the file exists.

quiz.q: Which character denotes a newline in many string literals?
quiz.why: \n separates lines when writing text.

quiz.q: Why might fields containing commas be enclosed in quotes in CSV?
options: To change the record's data type
To preserve the comma as part of one field
quiz.why: Quoting helps protect delimiter characters in CSV.

quiz.q: Which mode is normally used to inspect an existing text file without changing it?
quiz.why: Read mode is for inspecting or processing existing data.

quiz.q: Which is normally one record in a CSV file?
quiz.why: Each line typically represents one record.

quiz.q: Which keyword chooses the output columns in SQL?
quiz.why: SELECT lists the fields to return.

quiz.q: What does FROM identify?
quiz.why: FROM specifies the source table.

quiz.q: What does SELECT * request?
quiz.why: * in the SELECT list means all fields.

quiz.q: What does WHERE do?
quiz.why: WHERE restricts matching records.

quiz.q: Which condition matches rows where Age is at least 16?
quiz.why: The >= operator includes equality.

quiz.q: Which keyword sorts rows?
quiz.why: ORDER BY defines output ordering.

quiz.q: Which sort direction is descending?
quiz.why: DESC means descending order.

quiz.q: Which WHERE condition requires both conditions to hold?
quiz.why: AND requires both expressions.

quiz.q: In standard SQL, which pattern matches names starting with M?
quiz.why: % matches zero or more characters; the slides also demonstrate Access-style *.

quiz.q: Which SQL statement requests only the Title column from Books?
quiz.why: SELECT and FROM provide projection and source.

quiz.q: In a query, what does OR do?
options: Match when either condition is True
quiz.why: OR is True if at least one condition holds.

quiz.q: Which SQL condition selects pages from 100 to 200 inclusive?
quiz.why: BETWEEN includes its endpoints.

quiz.q: What helps stop SQL injection in applications?
options: Joining raw user text directly into SQL
quiz.why: Parameterisation keeps user data separate from SQL instructions.

quiz.q: Which query orders product names alphabetically?
options: SELECT ORDER BY Name FROM Products
SELECT Name FROM Products ORDER BY Name ASC
quiz.why: ORDER BY Name ASC sorts ascending.
